title: Terrorism: When the enemy is the state
gist: Twenty-five years after 9/11, the author argues the most overlooked predictor of violent extremism is the state itself — extremism in South and Southeast Asia grows out of local political conflicts, repression and weak state legitimacy rather than arriving as a foreign import — and warns that post-9/11 donor investment in state security capacity assumed states were responsible actors, when capability without accountability can make grievance production more efficient.

themes.theme: Extremism as a product of domestic political conditions, not foreign import

insights.claim: The 'terrorism as intruder' framing — arriving via unguarded borders, foreign-funded preachers, encrypted platforms or returning foreign fighters — is a comforting fiction that lets governments treat extremist violence as something happening to a country rather than something emerging from within its own politics.
insights.speaker: Simon Finley
insights.so_what: Challenges the standard counter-terrorism narrative used to justify border/surveillance-focused security spending — implies such spending alone will not resolve extremism rooted in domestic governance failures.
insights.quote: It is a comforting fiction. It allows governments to treat extremist violence as something that happens to a country rather than something that emerges from within its politics.
insights.locator: early paragraph on the intruder framing

insights.claim: Extremism in South and Southeast Asia is not an alien force entering peaceful societies — it grows out of local political conflicts, and while organisations and brand affiliations (e.g., pledges to Islamic State) may change, the underlying grievances do not.
insights.speaker: Simon Finley
insights.so_what: A framework for regional-risk analysts: track underlying local grievances (governance, land, discrimination) as the durable driver of extremism, not which global brand a group affiliates with at a given time.
insights.quote: Too often the brand was mistaken for the business.

insights.claim: In 2026, the Taliban is once again the government of Afghanistan, and across South and Southeast Asia groups that once pledged allegiance to Islamic State remain rooted in the same local conflicts that always sustained them — illustrating that the ideological brand offered publicity and access to a global network but did not transform local grievances into a genuinely global cause.
insights.speaker: Simon Finley
insights.so_what: Confirms persistence of Taliban rule and local-insurgency continuity as of 2026 — a baseline fact for regional stability/security-risk models covering Afghanistan and Islamic State-affiliated groups.
insights.locator: paragraph on Taliban and Islamic State-affiliated groups

themes.theme: Why radicalisation prediction fails but risk-location prediction works

insights.claim: Twenty-five years of research into childhood, education, religion, poverty, prisons, internet histories and psychology have failed to produce a reliable profile of who will become a terrorist, because radicalisation is highly individual, non-linear and shaped by countless personal experiences.
insights.speaker: Simon Finley
insights.so_what: Undercuts predictive-profiling approaches to counter-terrorism policy and screening — a caution against overinvesting in individual-level predictive surveillance/AI tools that claim to identify future terrorists.
insights.locator: paragraph on the conclusion of 25 years of research

insights.claim: While predicting who will embrace violence has proven remarkably difficult, identifying where violent movements flourish has become much easier: extremism thrives where unresolved conflict, political repression, human rights abuses, discrimination, corruption, weak state legitimacy and the absence of peaceful redress avenues create fertile ground.
insights.speaker: Simon Finley
insights.so_what: A geographic/structural risk-screening framework (governance quality indicators) that is more reliable than individual-profiling for forecasting where extremism will emerge — useful for country-risk models.

insights.claim: Countries most afflicted by violent extremism are also among those experiencing armed conflict, political terror and severe human rights abuses, because repression recruits more effectively than propaganda — state violence never excuses extremist violence, but it helps explain why extremist organisations continue finding recruits long after their ideology should have lost appeal.
insights.speaker: Simon Finley
insights.so_what: A direct causal claim linking state repression to extremist recruitment durability — relevant for assessing whether harder security crackdowns in a given country will reduce or perversely sustain insurgent recruitment.
insights.quote: Repression recruits more effectively than propaganda.

themes.theme: States as active sponsors of extremism and the post-9/11 aid blind spot

insights.claim: States have long funded, armed, sheltered and manipulated violent groups when it suited strategic interests — the US, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia supported Afghan fighters against Soviet forces during the Cold War, and Pakistan has long been accused of distinguishing between militant groups threatening the Pakistani state versus those advancing its interests in Afghanistan or India.
insights.speaker: Simon Finley
insights.so_what: Historical precedent for state-sponsored proxy extremism — relevant context for assessing continued risk of double-standard militant-group policies in South Asia today.
insights.locator: paragraph on Cold War state sponsorship

insights.claim: Donors invested heavily post-9/11 in making states better at fighting terrorism — training police, strengthening intelligence agencies, improving border management and expanding surveillance — but this rested on an assumption that the state itself was a responsible actor; capability without accountability may simply make the production of grievance more efficient, since an abusive security service equipped with better technology remains an abusive security service.
insights.speaker: Simon Finley
insights.so_what: A structural critique of two decades of counter-terrorism aid spending — implies donor governments and multilaterals should attach governance/accountability conditions to security-capacity funding rather than assuming capacity alone reduces terrorism risk.
insights.quote: Capability without accountability may simply make the production of grievance more efficient. An abusive security service equipped with better technology remains an abusive security service.

insights.claim: Heavy-handed policing, arbitrary detention, discrimination and political exclusion can operate like an overactive immune system, where the response becomes more dangerous than the disease — rather than isolating extremist organisations, such state overreach expands the audience willing to tolerate, support or join them.
insights.speaker: Simon Finley
insights.so_what: An 'overactive immune system' mental model for evaluating whether a government's counter-terrorism crackdown is net-reducing or net-increasing extremist recruitment — applicable to ongoing security operations across South/Southeast Asia.
insights.quote: Heavy-handed policing, arbitrary detention, discrimination and political exclusion can operate like an overactive immune system. The response becomes more dangerous than the disease.

insights.claim: A government cannot repress its way out of a conflict it helped create, cannot sponsor violent proxies abroad while condemning extremism at home, and cannot demand loyalty from citizens who encounter the state chiefly through corruption, discrimination or force.
insights.speaker: Simon Finley
insights.so_what: The article's summary policy conclusion — a template for judging the internal consistency (and likely effectiveness) of any government's counter-extremism strategy.
insights.quote: Sometimes the state is the solution. Sometimes it is part of the problem. Prevention begins with knowing the difference.
